This is a sensible way to validate demand before spending more. Freelancer or small agency setup Hiring help to configure a premium theme, load products, set up shipping and payments, and polish the main pages typically costs from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars, depending on catalogue size and how much design is involved. You get a faster, cleaner launch and fewer setup mistakes. Designed or custom store A store with a custom design, bespoke sections, integrations with stock or fulfilment systems, or complex product options can cost several thousand to tens of thousands of dollars. This suits established brands where the store's look and conversion rate move meaningful revenue. What ongoing costs should you plan for? The monthly Shopify plan. Card processing on every sale. App subscriptions: email, reviews, subscriptions, search, upsells. Review these every few months; unused apps are a common leak and can also slow the store. Theme updates and occasional developer help. Marketing: ads, email, content and SEO, which usually costs more over a year than the build itself. Where do small stores waste money? Too many apps at launch. Start with the essentials and add only when a real problem appears. Custom design before product-market fit. A premium theme done well is enough for most new stores. Skipping basics: clear product pages, shipping information and policies matter more than animations. See our guide to Shopify product pages . Ignoring search from day one. Clean titles, descriptions and URLs cost little at setup and are tedious to fix later; our Shopify SEO guide explains the basics. How do you estimate your own budget? A practical way to budget is to list each component in the table above and mark whether you will do it yourself, buy it or hire for it. Price the items you will buy from current published rates, ask two or three providers to quote the items you will hire for, and add the monthly costs for twelve months to see the first-year total. Then add a contingency, since most launches surface a few unplanned needs, such as an extra app, a shipping rule for a new region or a quick round of developer fixes. Compare that first-year figure with what you expect the store to earn. A new store testing demand should keep build costs small and leave most of the budget for marketing, because a beautiful store with no traffic sells nothing. An established business moving from another platform can justify spending more on design and migration, since it already has customers and revenue to protect. Is Shopify the right platform at all? Shopify is popular with small retailers because it handles hosting, security, checkout and payments in one place. Alternatives include WooCommerce on WordPress, Squarespace, Wix and BigCommerce, each with different trade-offs between cost, control and ease of use. Compare total costs, including apps and payment fees, rather than plan prices alone. What should you ask before hiring someone to build it? Will the store and all apps be registered to my account? Which theme will you use, and who pays for its licence? How many products, pages and revision rounds are included? Will you set up shipping, taxes, payments and legal policies? What training or handover do I get so I can run it myself? What ongoing app costs will I be left with? For a broader view of agency fees, see how much a marketing agency costs .

Q: Can I set up a Shopify store for free?
A: Not entirely. You can use a free theme and free apps, but you still pay a Shopify plan after any trial, plus payment processing and usually a domain.
Q: How much does it cost to hire someone to set up Shopify?
A: Roughly a few hundred to a few thousand dollars for a standard setup, more for custom design or integrations. Ranges vary widely.
Q: Do Shopify apps cost extra?
A: Many have free tiers, but paid apps are monthly subscriptions that can add up. Review them regularly.
Q: Should a new store pay for a custom theme?
A: Usually not at first. A well-configured premium or free theme is enough until the store has proven demand.
Q: Where can I check current Shopify plan prices?
A: On Shopify's own pricing page, which shows current plans and rates for your country.

### What are the red flags when hiring a marketing agency?
URL: https://smallbizwire.blog/marketing-agency-red-flags/
Published by Drifted Marketing. Author: SmallBizWire Editorial Team. Date: 2026-10-30.

Short answer: The biggest red flags are guaranteed results or rankings, an agency that wants your ad accounts or domain in its name, vague scope with no written deliverables, long lock-in contracts, no named people on your account, reports full of vanity metrics, unverifiable case studies and pressure to sign quickly. Any one deserves a direct question; several together mean walk away.

Most agencies are honest businesses doing difficult work. But marketing is easy to sell and hard to measure, and small businesses are the most exposed because they rarely have an in-house expert checking the agency's claims. These warning signs are worth knowing before the sales call, not after the first invoice. Do they guarantee results? Be very wary of guarantees such as "first page of Google in 30 days," "3x return on ad spend," or a fixed number of leads. Google itself states that no one can guarantee a ranking. Ad results depend on your product, price, stock, website and how fast you answer customers, none of which the agency controls. An honest agency commits to a measure, a target and a date to review, and explains what could stop it being hit. Do they want to own your accounts? If an agency insists on creating your ad account, analytics, domain or store under its own name, stop. You lose your data, audiences and history if you leave, and it gives the agency leverage over you. Legitimate agencies work inside accounts you own, added as a partner or user. Is the scope vague? "Full social media management" or "SEO services" with no numbers is not a scope. You should be able to read exactly what you get each month: how many posts, videos, campaigns, articles, reports and meetings. If the agency resists writing it down, the vagueness is the business model. Our contract checklist shows what a clear scope includes. Is there a long lock-in? A minimum term to give paid campaigns time to learn is reasonable. A twelve-month contract with heavy exit penalties and automatic renewal, for a small business trying an agency for the first time, is not. Ask for a shorter initial term or a clear exit if agreed targets are missed. Do you know who will actually do the work? A common pattern is a senior team in the pitch and juniors on the account. Ask who will run your work day to day, what their experience is, and whether you can meet them. If the answer is "a dedicated team" with no names, keep asking. Are the case studies verifiable? Results presented without client names, dates, context or references cannot be checked. That does not prove they are false, since some clients require confidentiality, but it means you should ask to speak with a current client in a business similar to yours. Be cautious of review profiles full of short, similar five-star reviews posted within a short period. Are the reports full of vanity metrics? Impressions, reach, followers and "engagement" can all rise while sales stay flat. A good report leads with the measures that connect to revenue: leads, orders, cost per acquisition, return on ad spend, and how they moved against the agreed target. If the agency cannot explain how its numbers relate to your sales, that is a warning. Are they marking up ad spend in secret? Some agencies pay ad platforms themselves and invoice you a higher amount without saying so. Insist that ad spend is billed by the platform to your own payment method, or that any management fee on spend is stated plainly. Are they pressuring you to sign? "This price is only valid today," or a discount for signing on the call, are sales tactics, not partnership signals. A good agency will give you time to read the contract and check references. Which tactics should worry you most? Buying followers, reviews or links. Fake reviews break platform rules and, in the US, can draw regulator attention; bought links can harm search rankings. Black-hat SEO such as hidden text, link schemes or mass-produced pages with no value. Spammy cold email from your domain with no authentication or opt-out, which can damage your sender reputation. Our guide to SPF, DKIM and DMARC explains why. Asking for your main passwords instead of using platform access tools. What does a quick red-flag scorecard look like? Warning sign What to ask Good answer Guaranteed results What exactly is guaranteed, and how? A measure, target and review date, not a promise Accounts in their name Whose name will the accounts be in? Yours, with them added as partner Vague scope What do I get each month, in numbers? A written list of deliverables Lock-in How do I leave, and what does it cost? A short notice period and clean handover Unknown team Who works on my account? Named people you can meet Unverifiable results Can I speak to a current client? Yes, with an introduction How long should you give an agency before judging it? Give paid campaigns around three months and SEO longer, but judge communication from week one. Missed deadlines, unanswered questions and reports that arrive late or say little are early signals that rarely improve on their own. Raise them directly, in writing, and note the response. What should you do if you already hired the wrong agency? First, make sure you hold owner access to every account: ad accounts, analytics, domain, hosting and store. If you do not, ask for ownership to be transferred before you raise anything else. Then download your reports, creative and files. Give notice in writing, following the contract's terms, and remove the agency's access on the agreed date. Change any passwords that were shared. Finally, write down what went wrong, so the next brief and contract cover it. Ending a poor engagement quickly usually costs less than hoping it improves. What are the green flags? The opposite of each warning: questions about your margins and customers before any proposal, a written scope, accounts in your name, named people, reports tied to revenue, honest talk about what might not work, and a willingness to start small. For the full process, see how to choose a marketing agency and our pricing guide .

Q: Is it a red flag if an agency guarantees first-page Google rankings?
A: Yes. Google states that no one can guarantee a ranking, so a guarantee suggests either misunderstanding or risky tactics.
Q: Should an agency own my ad account?
A: No. The account should be in your business's name, with the agency added as a partner or user.
Q: Are long agency contracts always bad?
A: Not always, but a long first contract with heavy exit penalties and automatic renewal is a warning sign for a small business.
Q: How can I check an agency's case studies?
A: Ask to speak with a current client in a business like yours, and look for named, dated results with context.
Q: What should an agency report each month?
A: Measures tied to revenue, such as leads, orders, cost per acquisition and return on ad spend, against an agreed target.

## Glossary

- SPF: Sender Policy Framework is an email authentication standard published as a DNS text record. It lists which mail servers are allowed to send email for your domain, so receiving servers can check whether a message claiming to be from you came from an approved source. It is one of the three core authentication records alongside DKIM and DMARC.
- DKIM: DomainKeys Identified Mail adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing email. The receiving server checks the signature against a public key published in your domain's DNS. A valid signature shows the message was authorised by the domain and was not altered in transit, which helps deliverability and protects against spoofing.
- DMARC: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance is a DNS policy that tells receiving servers what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM alignment checks: deliver it, quarantine it or reject it. It also sends reports to the domain owner, showing who is sending email using the domain.
- BIMI: Brand Indicators for Message Identification is a standard that lets a domain display its logo beside authenticated email in supporting inboxes. It requires a DMARC policy at enforcement, a logo in a specific SVG format, and for some mailbox providers a verified mark certificate. It rewards strong authentication with brand visibility.
- Sender reputation: Sender reputation is the trust mailbox providers place in a sending domain and IP address, based on signals such as spam complaints, bounces, engagement, authentication and sending patterns. A good reputation helps email reach the inbox; a poor one sends it to spam or gets it blocked. It builds slowly and can be damaged quickly.
- Warm-up: Warm-up is the practice of gradually increasing the volume of email sent from a new domain, mailbox or IP address over several weeks. Starting small and building steadily lets mailbox providers observe good behaviour before trusting larger volumes, reducing the chance that a sudden spike of email is treated as spam.
- Bounce rate (email): In email, bounce rate is the share of sent messages that could not be delivered. Hard bounces come from invalid or non-existent addresses; soft bounces are temporary, such as a full mailbox. A high bounce rate harms sender reputation, so lists should be verified and invalid addresses removed promptly. In web analytics the term means something different.
- Spam complaint rate: Spam complaint rate is the share of delivered emails that recipients mark as spam. Mailbox providers weigh it heavily. Google's sender guidelines ask bulk senders to keep it low, generally below 0.3 percent and ideally much lower. Clear consent, relevant content and an easy unsubscribe help keep complaints down.
- One-click unsubscribe: One-click unsubscribe lets a recipient opt out of marketing email with a single action, usually through a List-Unsubscribe header that the inbox shows as a button. Major mailbox providers such as Gmail and Yahoo require it for bulk senders of marketing email, and unsubscribe requests should be honoured promptly.
- NAP: NAP stands for name, address and phone number. For local search, a business's NAP should be identical everywhere it appears: its website, Google Business Profile, directories and social profiles. Consistent details help search engines confirm the business is real and located where it says, which supports local rankings.
- Google Business Profile: Google Business Profile is Google's free listing for businesses, shown in Google Search and Maps. It holds the business name, category, address or service area, hours, photos, reviews and posts. A complete, accurate and active profile is one of the most important factors in appearing for local searches.
- Map pack: The map pack is the block of local business results, usually three, shown with a map near the top of Google's results for searches with local intent, such as a service plus a city. Appearing there depends largely on relevance, distance and prominence, including the strength of a business's Google Business Profile.
- Local pack: Local pack is another name for the group of map-linked business listings that search engines show for local queries. The term is often used interchangeably with map pack. Businesses improve their chances of appearing through accurate profiles, relevant categories, reviews, consistent NAP details and locally relevant website content.
- Schema markup: Schema markup is structured data added to a web page, using the shared Schema.org vocabulary, to describe what the page is about: a product, a business, an article, an FAQ, an event. It helps search engines and other systems understand content and can make pages eligible for enhanced results.
- JSON-LD: JSON-LD, JavaScript Object Notation for Linked Data, is a format for adding structured data to a page inside a script tag, separate from the visible HTML. Google recommends it as the preferred way to add schema markup because it is easier to write and maintain than markup woven through the page.
- AEO: AEO, answer engine optimization, is the practice of structuring content so that search features and AI assistants can lift a clear, direct answer from it. It emphasises question-style headings, concise answers near the top, accurate facts and structured data, alongside conventional search optimization.
- GEO: GEO, generative engine optimization, refers to efforts to make content more likely to be cited or summarised by AI systems that generate answers, such as AI chat assistants and AI-powered search. The field is young and its methods are still debated; clear, well-sourced, accessible content is the common foundation.
- AI Overviews: AI Overviews are AI-generated summaries that Google shows at the top of some search results, with links to source pages. They answer a query directly, which can reduce clicks for some searches while giving cited sources visibility. Google says the usual search best practices apply to appearing in them.
- llms.txt: llms.txt is a proposed convention for a plain-text or Markdown file at a website's root that summarises the site and points AI models to its most useful pages. It is not an official standard, and support among AI providers is limited and uncertain, so it is best treated as an optional, low-cost addition.
- IndexNow: IndexNow is an open protocol that lets a website notify participating search engines, such as Bing and Yandex, the moment a page is added, updated or deleted, instead of waiting to be recrawled. It works by sending a simple request with the changed URLs and a key file hosted on the site. Google does not currently participate.
- Canonical URL: A canonical URL is the version of a page that a site tells search engines to treat as the main one when the same or very similar content is available at several addresses. It is set with a rel=canonical link tag and helps consolidate ranking signals and avoid duplicate-content confusion, common on e-commerce sites.
- CTR: CTR, click-through rate, is the percentage of people who click a link, ad or search result after seeing it, calculated as clicks divided by impressions. It indicates how compelling a headline, ad or listing is to the people who see it, though a high CTR matters only if those clicks go on to convert.
- CPC: CPC, cost per click, is the average amount an advertiser pays each time someone clicks an ad. It is calculated as total spend divided by clicks. CPC varies by platform, audience, industry and competition, and a cheap click is only valuable if it leads to customers at an acceptable cost.
- CPM: CPM, cost per mille, is the cost of one thousand ad impressions. It measures how expensive it is to reach an audience, regardless of clicks. Advertisers compare CPMs across platforms and audiences, and rising CPMs often signal more competition for the same people, for example during busy shopping seasons.
- ROAS: ROAS, return on ad spend, is revenue attributed to advertising divided by the cost of that advertising. A ROAS of 3 means three dollars of revenue per dollar spent. Because it uses revenue rather than profit, and depends on attribution settings, a business should judge it against its margins.
- CAC: CAC, customer acquisition cost, is the total cost of winning a new customer, including advertising, agency or staff costs, tools and promotions, divided by the number of new customers in the same period. Comparing CAC with lifetime value shows whether a business can afford its growth and which channels pay off.
- LTV: LTV, customer lifetime value, estimates the total revenue or, better, gross profit a business can expect from a customer over the whole relationship. It reflects order value, repeat purchases and retention. Businesses compare it with customer acquisition cost to decide how much they can sensibly spend to win a customer.
- Retainer: A retainer is a fixed monthly fee paid to an agency or consultant for an agreed scope of ongoing work, such as managing ads, producing content or SEO. It gives both sides predictable planning. A good retainer agreement lists the deliverables the fee buys, the reporting and the notice needed to end it.
- SOW: An SOW, statement of work, is a document describing a specific project or engagement: deliverables, timeline, responsibilities, acceptance criteria and fees. It often sits under a broader services agreement that holds the legal terms. A clear SOW prevents disputes by turning verbal promises into written commitments.
- Large language model: A large language model is an AI system trained on very large amounts of text to predict and generate language. It powers chat assistants that draft, summarise, translate and answer questions. Such models can write fluently but may state incorrect things confidently, so important outputs should be checked by a person.
- AI assistant: An AI assistant is software, usually powered by a large language model, that helps people with tasks through conversation: drafting messages, summarising documents, answering questions and organising work. For businesses, the safest pattern is that the assistant drafts and a person approves anything that is sent, paid or published.
- Prompt: A prompt is the instruction or question given to an AI model. Clear prompts state the task, the audience, the format wanted and any facts the model must use. Including examples and constraints usually produces more useful output than a short, vague request, and reduces the need for heavy editing afterwards.
- Hallucination: In AI, a hallucination is output that sounds plausible but is false or unsupported, such as an invented statistic, quote, citation or product detail. It happens because language models generate likely-sounding text rather than looking facts up. Checking claims against reliable sources before using them is the standard safeguard.
- Conversion rate: Conversion rate is the percentage of visitors or recipients who complete a desired action, such as a purchase, sign-up or enquiry, out of the total who had the chance. It is calculated as conversions divided by visitors. Small improvements can have a large effect on revenue without increasing traffic or ad spend.
- Landing page: A landing page is a web page built for a single purpose, usually where visitors arrive from an ad, email or search result. It focuses on one offer and one action, with a clear headline, supporting proof and a prominent call to action, and minimal distractions such as unrelated navigation links.
